question: How does the rocking accompaniment keep the tune airborne between its statements?
intro: The beginning of Die Walküre’s third act turns a rocking compound pulse into the Valkyries’ riding music. This short acoustic Edison record presents an orchestral concert excerpt, not the full scene with its Valkyrie voices.

cues.title: A rocking foundation
cues.text: The written riding music sets a strongly profiled tune against a restless compound-time accompaniment. Follow the underlying swing before concentrating on the famous melody; this orchestral excerpt removes the Valkyries’ sung calls.
cues.evidence: General description of the Act III opening. The NPS source identifies the orchestral Edison excerpt, not a vocal performance.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: An Edison orchestra
cues.text: The National Park Service dates this American Symphony Orchestra recording to 1921 and its release to December of that year. The name identifies an early recording ensemble, not the orchestra founded by Leopold Stokowski in 1962.
cues.evidence: https://www.nps.gov/edis/learn/photosmultimedia/classical-instrumental.htm documents recording and release dates; no conductor is credited. The modern orchestra’s foundation is a separate institutional identity.

cues.title: Two layers of motion
cues.text: Across the riding music, distinguish the broad tune from the quicker accompaniment beneath it. The tune can sustain or repeat a note while the underlying figure keeps the motion continuous.
cues.evidence: General listening prompt about the riding theme’s characteristic layered texture; no instrumental entrance is claimed for 1:04.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Less weight then renewed force
cues.text: The recorded level falls in the preceding stretch, then rises again. Listen for the riding character to remain recognisable when the texture is less forceful; intensity and thematic identity are different things.

cues.title: Before the complete Ring
cues.text: Die Walküre first reaches the stage in Munich in 1870, six years before the complete Ring cycle at Bayreuth. The concert excerpt gives the riding music an independent life outside its dramatic setting.
cues.evidence: Wagner work chronology in the site biography; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Die_Walk%C3%BCre documents Munich 1870 and Bayreuth 1876.

cues.title: Surges replace a steady plateau
cues.text: The later part alternates stronger attacks with local withdrawals instead of simply remaining loud. Track those changes against the continuing pulse: each fresh increase can renew the riding gesture without introducing a new tune.
cues.evidence: Analysis boundaries 2:44, 2:52 and 3:02; levels alternate −12.4 at 2:40, −18 at 2:45, −11.5 at 2:50 and −19.5 at 3:00.

cues.title: The late crest
cues.text: This late span contains the recording’s strongest measured window. Compare its weight with the earlier statements, while keeping the accompaniment’s motion in the foreground of your attention.
cues.evidence: Analysis: loudest five-second window at 3:05, −10.8 dB; the following 3:20 span remains strong at −11.8 dB.

cues.title: A processed historical transfer
cues.text: The current Commons file credits hiss reduction and equalisation, with a beat removed near the start. Those transfer decisions belong to the digital copy, not to Wagner’s score or an instruction for the 1921 players.
cues.evidence: Commons current-file upload history and description: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Richard_Wagner_-_Ride_of_the_Valkyries.ogg; Adam Cuerden’s noise-removal/equalisation version.

cues.title: An ending made for the excerpt
cues.text: The concert extract reaches its own stopping point. In the opera, the Valkyries’ gathering belongs to a continuing scene; here the final attacks and their decay close a single record-length performance.
cues.evidence: NPS identifies “The Valkyrie—Ride of the Valkyries”, Edison 80638-R. Analysis falls from −13.8 dB at 4:05 to −49.9 dB at 4:15. Exact arranger and cuts are unestablished.

transitions.title: Accumulation opens into a broad statement
transitions.how: A rising recorded level carries the opening into the first sustained strong span. The riding theme and its quicker accompaniment work at different rhythmic scales, so the broader melodic statement does not cancel the underlying motion. The precise acoustic arrangement is unidentified.
transitions.evidence: Analysis boundaries at 0:40 and 0:48; level rises from −32.8 dB at the start to approximately −13 dB by 0:25–0:50.

transitions.title: The intensity recedes without stopping
transitions.how: The sound loses weight after the first broad span, making room for a later renewal. The contrast lies in changing weight and texture while the excerpt continues.
transitions.evidence: Analysis boundary 1:20 and lower levels at 1:20–1:30; no individual harmonic event is inferred from chroma.

transitions.title: A continuing pulse supports renewed surges
transitions.how: The later span renews its force through successive rises separated by brief reductions. Familiar rhythmic material links the surges, while the alternation of lighter and heavier textures refreshes the broad riding gesture.
transitions.evidence: Analysis strongest boundary at 2:44, with further changes at 2:52 and 3:02; passage-level description.

transitions.title: The concert span reaches its close
transitions.how: The late strong span gives way to the excerpt’s closing gestures and their decay.
transitions.evidence: Analysis boundary 4:00, relatively strong windows through 4:05, then falling level and near-silence by 4:15. The source establishes a self-contained orchestral record but not its arranger; a particular operatic bar or concert-ending cadence is not assigned to this boundary.

composer.epithet: An opera composer who made the orchestra remember what the characters conceal, and built a theatre for the result.
facts: Composition with Theodor Weinlig in Leipzig; practical theatre work in Würzburg, Magdeburg, Königsberg and Riga
Royal Saxon Kapellmeister, Dresden, 1843–49; founder of the Bayreuth Festival, first held in 1876
Wrote his own librettos, alongside extensive and often polemical prose
Thirteen completed operas; the four-part Ring; songs, orchestral works and piano music
composer.background:
Wagner grew up among actors, singers and theatrical households in Leipzig and Dresden. His father died in 1813; his mother subsequently married the actor and painter Ludwig Geyer. Literature preceded serious musical training: as a schoolboy Wagner attempted a tragedy before he had mastered composition. Beethoven’s symphonies and Weber’s operas supplied different models, one for the weight of an orchestral argument, the other for a German theatre of supernatural events and sharply characterised instruments. Lessons with Theodor Weinlig in 1831 gave him a grounding in counterpoint. The later claim to have rebuilt opera came from someone who first learned its routines as a working theatre musician.

He held posts in Würzburg, Magdeburg, Königsberg and Riga, married the actress Minna Planer in 1836, and repeatedly found himself in debt. His early operas tried incompatible languages: Die Feen follows German Romantic opera, while Das Liebesverbot, after Shakespeare’s Measure for Measure, adopts a more Italianate manner. In 1839 the Wagners fled Riga and travelled by sea to London, then to Paris. There he copied, arranged and wrote journalism while trying to enter the operatic establishment. Meyerbeer, whom Wagner would later attack, helped him obtain a hearing for Rienzi. Wagner knew the grand-opera machinery of public ceremony, political catastrophe and large chorus from practical experience.
